title: Three canons
hook: the Pali canon, the Chinese canon and the Tibetan canon

segments.voice: Yesterday, sudden and gradual: two verses on a wall, a slow ocean floor, and Bahiya freed in the street. Your line was both are true. Did anything land all at once? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-three.

Near the end of his life, in the Pali account of his last days, the Buddha sees a worry coming. When he is gone, someone will say: our teacher is finished, we have no teacher anymore. Not so, he tells Ananda. The teaching and the discipline he has given them will be their teacher after he is gone. So the monks did what people do with a teacher they cannot afford to lose. They remembered. They recited together. Later, the words were written down. And in different lands, the remembering took different shapes. Today: three canons.
screen: `WE HAVE NO TEACHER.` → `NOT SO.` → `THE TEACHING WILL BE YOUR TEACHER.`

segments.voice: A canon is a collection a community treats as its scripture. Buddhists keep three great ones, each in its own language, each with its own shape. First, the Pali canon, kept by the Theravada schools of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. Its name is the Tipitaka, which tradition explains as three baskets: one for the monastic discipline, one for the discourses, one for the higher teaching called Abhidhamma. Theravada tradition says it was handed down by memory for a long time before it was written. Second, the Chinese canon, sometimes called the great storehouse of scriptures. It holds texts translated from Indian languages, including collections of early discourses called the Agamas, which run close to the Pali ones. Readers can lay the two side by side and find the same story, told with small differences. It also holds Mahayana sutras, monastic codes, and works first written in China, such as the Platform Sutra from yesterday. It was read across China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam. Third, the Tibetan canon, in two parts. The Kangyur gathers what Tibetan tradition counts as the Buddha's own word, in translation. The Tengyur gathers commentaries and treatises by later Indian teachers. Tibetan translators worked closely from Indian texts. Now lay the three side by side. They overlap far more than their covers suggest. A monk in Bangkok, a nun in Taipei and a lama in Dharamsala can each open their own canon and find the Buddha teaching the four truths. The wording differs. The bookshelves differ. The teacher, in the Buddha's own sense, is the same.
screen: `PALI: THREE BASKETS.` · `CHINESE: A GREAT STOREHOUSE.` · `TIBETAN: THE WORD AND THE COMMENTS.` · `THE SAME TEACHER, THREE SHELVES.` · then, large: `THREE CANONS.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, sit and let the breath settle. Name the first canon quietly: the Pali canon. Picture someone reading it this morning, in a monastery in Sri Lanka or Thailand. Breathe. Name the second: the Chinese canon. Picture a reader in Seoul or Kyoto turning the page. Breathe. Name the third: the Tibetan canon. Picture a long cloth-wrapped book being unwrapped on a table. Breathe. Then sit with the thought the Buddha left Ananda: the teaching itself as the teacher. The bell holds the time.
Three canons. The Pali, the Chinese and the Tibetan collections of scripture, each its own library, often holding the same teachings in different words. Today's word.
Your line: three canons. Today, when you pick up any book you trust, notice who kept it for you, and how. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Theravada communities study and chant from the Pali canon, East Asian Buddhists draw on the Chinese canon, and Tibetan and Himalayan Buddhists use the Kangyur and Tengyur, often keeping the volumes wrapped in cloth on the temple shelf.

pairs: early discourses in the Chinese canon

myth: the three canons share no teachings at all
they overlap: all three hold the Buddha teaching the four truths, in different words.
in the Pali account of his last days, the Buddha says the teaching will be the teacher
he tells Ananda the teaching and discipline will be their teacher after he is gone.
the Chinese canon holds only texts written in China
it holds many translations from Indian languages, along with works first written in China.

fork.setup: you're Ananda. the Buddha is near the end of his life, and some fear they'll have no teacher. what does he tell you?
options: choose a new teacher to lead you.
the teaching and discipline will be your teacher.
wait for the next Buddha to come.
fork.reveal: he names no successor. the teaching itself is to be the teacher, and the canons are how communities kept it.

original.note: Pali Tipitaka, the name of the Pali canon, which tradition explains as three baskets.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism has one bible.
what it means: there are three great canons, Pali, Chinese and Tibetan, each its own library, overlapping in much of what they teach.
what a scholar hears: the Tipitaka's three baskets, the Chinese Agamas running close to the Pali discourses, and the Kangyur and Tengyur.

notes: DN 16 paraphrased: the dhamma and vinaya as teacher after the Buddha's passing; confirm.
'Tipitaka, which tradition explains as three baskets' and the three divisions; confirm.
'Handed down by memory for a long time before it was written' given as Theravada tradition, no date; confirm.
Chinese canon called 'the great storehouse of scriptures' (Dazangjing); Agamas parallel the Pali Nikayas; confirm wording.
Kangyur as the Buddha's word in translation, Tengyur as Indian commentaries and treatises; 'some works lost in their original language survive there'; confirm.
Places named (Bangkok, Taipei, Dharamsala, Seoul, Kyoto) are illustrative; confirm the Chinese canon was read in Korea, Japan and Vietnam.
Original: तिपिटक; confirm spelling and pronunciation.
